note.note:
Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
- 65-year-old man with acute, ongoing central chest pressure radiating to left arm/shoulder, associated diaphoresis, dyspnoea, and nausea; emergency services activated for presumed acute coronary syndrome (ACS).

History:
- Presenting complaint: Sudden onset chest “pressure, like someone sitting on my chest” began while gardening ~2 h ago; still present.
- Associated symptoms: Left arm/shoulder pain, shortness of breath, nausea (no vomiting), sweating, perceived tachycardia.
- Pertinent negatives: No prior similar episodes; no jaw/neck pain reported; no vomiting.
- Past medical history: Hypertension; no diabetes; cholesterol never checked.
- Allergies: Aspirin – mild swelling reaction.
- Medications: Not discussed.
- Family history: Father died of MI ~age 60; mother with unspecified heart problems.
- Social / preventive: Smokes 10 cigarettes/day × 15 y; drinks ~7–8 pints beer/week; overweight; low physical activity; lives alone; restaurant owner.

Examination:
- Telehealth visual impression: Diaphoretic and appears short of breath.
- Vitals: Not available.
- No further physical findings documented.

Impression:
- Most likely: Acute coronary syndrome (myocardial infarction/unstable angina) – classic exertion-related central pressure, left-arm radiation, diaphoresis, nausea, multiple CAD risk factors.
- Alternate but less likely considerations: 
  • Aortic dissection – hypertension/smoking; pain quality and absence of back radiation make this less probable.  
  • Pulmonary embolism – acute SOB, but pain not pleuritic and risk profile favors ACS.

Plan:
- Emergency management: Ambulance dispatched; clinician remained on call until arrival.
- Expected ED care: Pre-hospital ECG, cardiac monitoring, possible antiplatelet therapy (team alerted to aspirin allergy), serial cardiac enzymes, and definitive hospital placement per ECG findings.
- Patient instructions: Keep front door open for paramedics; communicate aspirin allergy details to EMS/Hospital staff.
- Follow-up: Will depend on hospital assessment; no outpatient follow-up arranged at this time due to emergent transfer.

Quality checks:

● Missing/expected data:
  – Current medications list.  
  – Objective vital signs, ECG, labs.  
  – Weight/BMI, complete cardiovascular risk assessment.  
  – Formal follow-up plan post-hospitalization.

● Transcript/DDx conflicts:
  – Minor age discrepancy in conversation; DOB 08-Aug-1958 ⇒ 65 y, though patient/doctor referenced “about 60.”  
  – No other conflicts noted.

● Transcript quality:
  – Clear description of key symptoms and risk factors; lacks objective exam findings and medication list typical of emergency teleconsult.
